cheat_sheet.title: Web and HTML Foundations — Structural Cheat Sheet
cheat_sheet.introduction: This sheet turns Web and HTML Foundations into visible relationships. It is a reference for planning, tracing, debugging, and explaining—not a list to memorize.
cheat_sheet.why_it_matters: The level contributes directly to a responsive web application. Each concept helps the learner move from an ambiguous task to a contract, a representation, a verified transition, and an explainable result.

mental_model.summary: Represent the work as a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions before translating it into implementation details.
reasoning_cycle: Model variables, state, constraints, and relationships

input_questions: What may be absent or malformed?
output_questions: What shape and state are promised?

core_concepts.title: Lists, tables, and structured records

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.

Is the boundary inclusive or exclusive?
Can an invalid or repeated event mutate valid state?
Are asynchronous or external results stale, missing, or out of order?
Does the representation match the operation mix and constraints?
Did the repair pass the original failure and nearby regression cases?

lessons.title: Web requests and browser rendering
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Web requests and browser rendering within an accessible browser interface.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Web requests and browser rendering to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Web requests and browser rendering is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A URL identifies a resource; the browser requests it, interprets the response, builds internal trees, and renders pixels.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Web requests and browser rendering, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Web requests and browser rendering
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.name: candidate_input
variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.name: constraint_result
variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: A URL identifies a resource; the browser requests it, interprets the response, builds internal trees, and renders pixels.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.
List state variables and separate current state from a candidate update.
Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.
Apply the structural rule for Web requests and browser rendering.
Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

worked_examples.title: Normal case: contract to verified output
worked_examples.scenario: A learner applies Web requests and browser rendering while building an accessible browser interface.
worked_examples.input: One well-formed input that satisfies the documented preconditions.
reasoning: Name the observable output before choosing an operation.
Represent only the state and relationships needed for that output.
A URL identifies a resource; the browser requests it, interprets the response, builds internal trees, and renders pixels.
Trace the transition and compare the result with the contract.
worked_examples.output: A valid state transition with the promised result and recorded evidence.

worked_examples.title: Boundary case: valid at the limit
worked_examples.scenario: The input is exactly at the smallest or largest documented valid boundary.
worked_examples.input: A boundary value explicitly included by the constraint.
reasoning: Write the inclusive or exclusive boundary symbolically.
Evaluate the predicate before changing state.
Apply the same rule used for ordinary valid input.
Verify that the output remains representable and accessible.
worked_examples.output: The boundary case is accepted once and produces a valid output without special hidden state.

worked_examples.title: Rejected case: preserve the invariant
worked_examples.scenario: An input violates one required relationship or arrives in an unsupported state.
worked_examples.input: An out-of-contract value paired with a previously valid state.
reasoning: Identify the failed constraint and stop before commit.
Keep the previous valid state unchanged.
Return a specific, non-sensitive explanation or recovery path.
Record the case as evidence for a regression check.
worked_examples.output: A controlled rejection, preserved prior state, and actionable feedback.

structured_representation.caption: A validate-before-commit trace for Web requests and browser rendering.

common_mistakes: Beginning implementation before defining the required output.
Changing state before the input or transition has been validated.
Memorizing the label 'Web requests and browser rendering' without applying its governing relationship.
Testing only one convenient normal case and assuming boundaries behave identically.
edge_cases: The smallest valid input or empty valid structure, when allowed.
The largest documented input, count, depth, size, or duration.
A duplicate, repeated event, retry, or already-completed transition.
Malformed, missing, stale, unauthorized, or otherwise out-of-contract input.
debugging_strategy: Freeze the first input that produces a wrong observable result.
Write the expected trace beside the observed trace.
Locate the first row where state, constraint, or output diverges.
Repair the rule or boundary responsible for that first divergence.
Rerun the failing case plus one normal, one boundary, and one rejection case.
progressive_hints: Label the input and promised output before naming any tool or syntax.
Separate current_state from next_state and write the validity predicate.
Apply this rule, then trace the boundary: A URL identifies a resource; the browser requests it, interprets the response, builds internal trees, and renders pixels.
lessons.summary: Web requests and browser rendering is mastered when the learner can model its inputs and state, apply the rule 'A URL identifies a resource; the browser requests it, interprets the response, builds internal trees, and renders pixels.', and prove the result with normal, boundary, and rejected traces.

lessons.title: Semantic document skeleton
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Semantic document skeleton within an accessible browser interface.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Semantic document skeleton to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Semantic document skeleton is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A valid page separates metadata from visible content and uses landmarks that communicate each region's purpose.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Semantic document skeleton, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Semantic document skeleton
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract

project.title: Web and HTML Foundations: Responsive Web Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs an accessible browser interface that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate responsive web application that demonstrates all eight skills from Web and HTML Foundations. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A URL identifies a resource; the browser requests it, interprets the response, builds internal trees, and renders pixels.
A valid page separates metadata from visible content and uses landmarks that communicate each region's purpose.
HTML elements form a rooted tree: every non-root node has one parent, and correct nesting preserves the intended hierarchy.
Content elements carry meaning, while relative and absolute paths determine how a browser locates linked resources.
Choose lists for sequences and tables for genuinely two-dimensional relationships with explicit headers.
A form maps labeled user inputs to named values, applies constraints, and submits a predictable record.
Names, roles, relationships, focus order, and alternatives make the same structure perceivable without relying on sight or a pointer.
Debug from document structure outward: validate markup, inspect paths, test interaction order, then verify the deployed response.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Web requests and browser rendering and cite its governing rule in the decision record.

constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

maximum documented size
duplicate or retry

debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

core_concepts.title: Cascade, specificity, and inheritance
core_concepts.rule: The winning declaration is determined by origin, importance, specificity, and source order; only inheritable properties flow from parent to child.

core_concepts.title: Box model and predictable sizing
core_concepts.rule: Rendered size is the sum of content, padding, border, and margin unless border-box sizing moves padding and border inside the declared dimensions.

core_concepts.title: Selectors, combinators, and UI states
core_concepts.rule: Selectors describe sets of nodes and relationships; narrowly target stable structure without encoding accidental nesting.

core_concepts.title: Normal flow, display, and positioning
core_concepts.rule: Normal flow places boxes in document order; positioning should change a box's reference relationship only when the design requires it.

core_concepts.title: Flexbox axes and alignment
core_concepts.rule: Flexbox distributes items along one main axis and aligns them along the cross axis under available-space constraints.

core_concepts.title: Grid tracks and two-dimensional layout
core_concepts.rule: Grid defines row and column tracks, then places items into cells or named regions while preserving explicit spatial relationships.

core_concepts.title: Responsive constraints and media queries
core_concepts.rule: Responsive design selects fluid defaults and introduces breakpoints where content constraints—not device names—stop being satisfied.

core_concepts.title: Design tokens, accessibility, and CSS debugging
core_concepts.rule: Reusable tokens keep visual relationships consistent; contrast, focus, zoom, and inspector checks protect usability across states.

lessons.title: Cascade, specificity, and inheritance
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Cascade, specificity, and inheritance within an accessible browser interface.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Cascade, specificity, and inheritance to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Cascade, specificity, and inheritance is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. The winning declaration is determined by origin, importance, specificity, and source order; only inheritable properties flow from parent to child.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Cascade, specificity, and inheritance, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Normal flow, display, and positioning to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Normal flow, display, and positioning is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Normal flow places boxes in document order; positioning should change a box's reference relationship only when the design requires it.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Normal flow, display, and positioning, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Design tokens, accessibility, and CSS debugging is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Reusable tokens keep visual relationships consistent; contrast, focus, zoom, and inspector checks protect usability across states.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Design tokens, accessibility, and CSS debugging, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Modern CSS and Responsive Design: Responsive Web Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs an accessible browser interface that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate responsive web application that demonstrates all eight skills from Modern CSS and Responsive Design. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: The winning declaration is determined by origin, importance, specificity, and source order; only inheritable properties flow from parent to child.
Rendered size is the sum of content, padding, border, and margin unless border-box sizing moves padding and border inside the declared dimensions.
Selectors describe sets of nodes and relationships; narrowly target stable structure without encoding accidental nesting.
Normal flow places boxes in document order; positioning should change a box's reference relationship only when the design requires it.
Flexbox distributes items along one main axis and aligns them along the cross axis under available-space constraints.
Grid defines row and column tracks, then places items into cells or named regions while preserving explicit spatial relationships.
Responsive design selects fluid defaults and introduces breakpoints where content constraints—not device names—stop being satisfied.
Reusable tokens keep visual relationships consistent; contrast, focus, zoom, and inspector checks protect usability across states.

core_concepts.title: Values, types, and explicit conversion
core_concepts.rule: A value has a type that determines valid operations; explicit conversion makes input assumptions visible and testable.

core_concepts.title: Variables, expressions, and state
core_concepts.rule: A variable names a current value, while an expression maps existing values to a new result without changing unrelated state.

core_concepts.title: Boolean logic and branching
core_concepts.rule: A branch partitions possible states by predicates; conditions must be mutually understood and boundary cases tested.

core_concepts.title: Loops, counters, and invariants
core_concepts.rule: A loop needs an initial state, continuation condition, update, and invariant that remains true after every iteration.

core_concepts.title: Functions as input-output mappings
core_concepts.rule: A function defines a reusable contract from parameters to a return value or documented effect, with scope limiting accidental dependencies.

core_concepts.title: Arrays and sequence transformations
core_concepts.rule: Arrays model ordered data; map, filter, find, and reduce express distinct transformations with predictable output shapes.

core_concepts.title: Objects, records, and lookup
core_concepts.rule: Objects group named fields into records; safe access and deliberate updates preserve the record's expected shape.

core_concepts.title: DOM events and interface state
core_concepts.rule: An event supplies input, a handler computes a state transition, and rendering makes the new state visible in the document tree.

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.

lessons.title: Boolean logic and branching
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Boolean logic and branching within an accessible browser interface.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Boolean logic and branching to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Boolean logic and branching is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A branch partitions possible states by predicates; conditions must be mutually understood and boundary cases tested.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Boolean logic and branching, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.title: Arrays and sequence transformations
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Arrays and sequence transformations within an accessible browser interface.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Arrays and sequence transformations to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Arrays and sequence transformations is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Arrays model ordered data; map, filter, find, and reduce express distinct transformations with predictable output shapes.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Arrays and sequence transformations, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

project.title: JavaScript and Programming Logic: Responsive Web Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs an accessible browser interface that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate responsive web application that demonstrates all eight skills from JavaScript and Programming Logic. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A value has a type that determines valid operations; explicit conversion makes input assumptions visible and testable.
A variable names a current value, while an expression maps existing values to a new result without changing unrelated state.
A branch partitions possible states by predicates; conditions must be mutually understood and boundary cases tested.
A loop needs an initial state, continuation condition, update, and invariant that remains true after every iteration.
A function defines a reusable contract from parameters to a return value or documented effect, with scope limiting accidental dependencies.
Arrays model ordered data; map, filter, find, and reduce express distinct transformations with predictable output shapes.
Objects group named fields into records; safe access and deliberate updates preserve the record's expected shape.
An event supplies input, a handler computes a state transition, and rendering makes the new state visible in the document tree.

starter_materials.scaffold_policy: Level 3 leaves architecture and core transitions partially open.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Values, types, and explicit conversion and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Variables, expressions, and state and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Boolean logic and branching and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Loops, counters, and invariants and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Functions as input-output mappings and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Arrays and sequence transformations and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Objects, records, and lookup and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate DOM events and interface state and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

maximum documented size
duplicate or retry

malformed or unauthorized input

Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Asynchronous timelines and promises within an accessible browser interface.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Asynchronous timelines and promises to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Asynchronous timelines and promises is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A promise represents a future result; awaiting it orders dependent work without blocking unrelated browser tasks.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Asynchronous timelines and promises, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

lessons.title: API-driven application architecture
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend API-driven application architecture within an accessible browser interface.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use API-driven application architecture to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: API-driven application architecture is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Separate transport, validation, domain state, and rendering so each layer has one responsibility and failures stay localized.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For API-driven application architecture, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates API-driven application architecture
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Separate transport, validation, domain state, and rendering so each layer has one responsibility and failures stay localized.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.

project.title: Advanced JavaScript, APIs and Browser Data: Responsive Web Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs an accessible browser interface that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate responsive web application that demonstrates all eight skills from Advanced JavaScript, APIs and Browser Data. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A promise represents a future result; awaiting it orders dependent work without blocking unrelated browser tasks.
A network request is not complete at receipt: code must inspect status, parse the expected body, and handle transport and application failures separately.
External JSON is untrusted structured data; validate required fields and types before allowing it to update application state.
Loading, success, empty, and failure are distinct states; retries must be bounded and safe for the operation being repeated.
Choose memory, session, or persistent storage by lifetime, sensitivity, capacity, and synchronization needs.
Modules expose small public contracts and hide internal details, producing a directed dependency graph that is easier to test.
Non-mutating transformations create a new value from old state, making change histories and UI updates easier to reason about.
Separate transport, validation, domain state, and rendering so each layer has one responsibility and failures stay localized.

core_concepts.title: Components, JSX, and render trees
core_concepts.rule: A component maps inputs and current state to a declarative subtree; composition builds the full interface tree.

core_concepts.title: Props, contracts, and composition
core_concepts.rule: Props are read-only inputs; clear prop contracts and composition keep parent-child responsibilities explicit.

core_concepts.title: State, identity, and render transitions
core_concepts.rule: State belongs at the nearest common owner, and stable identity determines whether React preserves or replaces a component's state.

core_concepts.title: Events, controlled forms, and reducers
core_concepts.rule: User events become actions; controlled values or reducers make each transition from previous state to next state explicit.

core_concepts.title: Effects and synchronized external systems
core_concepts.rule: An effect synchronizes rendering with an external system and needs accurate dependencies plus cleanup for obsolete work.

core_concepts.title: Routing and shared application state
core_concepts.rule: Routes form a navigation graph; only genuinely shared state should move above local component boundaries.

core_concepts.title: Testing, accessibility, and performance
core_concepts.rule: Test observable behavior, measure before optimizing, and preserve accessible names, focus, and feedback across every state.

core_concepts.title: Build, deployment, and maintainable architecture
core_concepts.rule: A deployable frontend has reproducible builds, environment separation, monitored assets, and clear layer boundaries.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Components, JSX, and render trees is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A component maps inputs and current state to a declarative subtree; composition builds the full interface tree.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Components, JSX, and render trees, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.

Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Props are read-only inputs; clear prop contracts and composition keep parent-child responsibilities explicit.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Props, contracts, and composition, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use a document tree, layout constraints, and user-driven state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Props, contracts, and composition
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.name: candidate_input
variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.name: constraint_result
variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Props are read-only inputs; clear prop contracts and composition keep parent-child responsibilities explicit.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.
List state variables and separate current state from a candidate update.
Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.
Apply the structural rule for Props, contracts, and composition.
Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

worked_examples.title: Normal case: contract to verified output
worked_examples.scenario: A learner applies Props, contracts, and composition while building an accessible browser interface.
worked_examples.input: One well-formed input that satisfies the documented preconditions.
reasoning: Name the observable output before choosing an operation.
Represent only the state and relationships needed for that output.
Props are read-only inputs; clear prop contracts and composition keep parent-child responsibilities explicit.
Trace the transition and compare the result with the contract.
worked_examples.output: A valid state transition with the promised result and recorded evidence.

worked_examples.title: Boundary case: valid at the limit
worked_examples.scenario: The input is exactly at the smallest or largest documented valid boundary.
worked_examples.input: A boundary value explicitly included by the constraint.
reasoning: Write the inclusive or exclusive boundary symbolically.
Evaluate the predicate before changing state.
Apply the same rule used for ordinary valid input.
Verify that the output remains representable and accessible.
worked_examples.output: The boundary case is accepted once and produces a valid output without special hidden state.

worked_examples.title: Rejected case: preserve the invariant
worked_examples.scenario: An input violates one required relationship or arrives in an unsupported state.
worked_examples.input: An out-of-contract value paired with a previously valid state.
reasoning: Identify the failed constraint and stop before commit.
Keep the previous valid state unchanged.
Return a specific, non-sensitive explanation or recovery path.
Record the case as evidence for a regression check.
worked_examples.output: A controlled rejection, preserved prior state, and actionable feedback.

structured_representation.caption: A validate-before-commit trace for Props, contracts, and composition.

common_mistakes: Beginning implementation before defining the required output.
Changing state before the input or transition has been validated.
Memorizing the label 'Props, contracts, and composition' without applying its governing relationship.
Testing only one convenient normal case and assuming boundaries behave identically.
edge_cases: The smallest valid input or empty valid structure, when allowed.
The largest documented input, count, depth, size, or duration.
A duplicate, repeated event, retry, or already-completed transition.
Malformed, missing, stale, unauthorized, or otherwise out-of-contract input.
debugging_strategy: Freeze the first input that produces a wrong observable result.
Write the expected trace beside the observed trace.
Locate the first row where state, constraint, or output diverges.
Repair the rule or boundary responsible for that first divergence.
Rerun the failing case plus one normal, one boundary, and one rejection case.
progressive_hints: Label the input and promised output before naming any tool or syntax.
Separate current_state from next_state and write the validity predicate.
Apply this rule, then trace the boundary: Props are read-only inputs; clear prop contracts and composition keep parent-child responsibilities explicit.
lessons.summary: Props, contracts, and composition is mastered when the learner can model its inputs and state, apply the rule 'Props are read-only inputs; clear prop contracts and composition keep parent-child responsibilities explicit.', and prove the result with normal, boundary, and rejected traces.

activities.prompt: A fictional implementation of Props, contracts, and composition accepts an out-of-contract input and overwrites a valid previous state. Select the repair that validates before mutation and preserves the previous state on rejection.

options.text: Mutate first, then hide any error message.
Validate the candidate, compute a new state, commit only if valid, otherwise retain the previous state.
Delete the constraint so every input becomes valid.
Retry the same mutation until it appears to work.

activities.explanation: Validation before commit makes rejection side-effect-free and preserves the state invariant.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Events, controlled forms, and reducers is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Events, controlled forms, and reducers, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Testing, accessibility, and performance is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Test observable behavior, measure before optimizing, and preserve accessible names, focus, and feedback across every state.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Testing, accessibility, and performance, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship

Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Build, deployment, and maintainable architecture, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: React, Architecture, Testing and Deployment: Responsive Web Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs an accessible browser interface that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate responsive web application that demonstrates all eight skills from React, Architecture, Testing and Deployment. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A component maps inputs and current state to a declarative subtree; composition builds the full interface tree.
Props are read-only inputs; clear prop contracts and composition keep parent-child responsibilities explicit.
State belongs at the nearest common owner, and stable identity determines whether React preserves or replaces a component's state.
User events become actions; controlled values or reducers make each transition from previous state to next state explicit.
An effect synchronizes rendering with an external system and needs accurate dependencies plus cleanup for obsolete work.
Routes form a navigation graph; only genuinely shared state should move above local component boundaries.
Test observable behavior, measure before optimizing, and preserve accessible names, focus, and feedback across every state.
A deployable frontend has reproducible builds, environment separation, monitored assets, and clear layer boundaries.

starter_materials.scaffold_policy: Level 5 supplies only constraints, acceptance criteria, and review checkpoints.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Components, JSX, and render trees and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Props, contracts, and composition and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate State, identity, and render transitions and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Events, controlled forms, and reducers and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Effects and synchronized external systems and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Routing and shared application state and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Testing, accessibility, and performance and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Build, deployment, and maintainable architecture and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.expected: one correct output and valid next state

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

edge_cases: empty or minimum
maximum documented size
duplicate or retry
out-of-order or stale result
malformed or unauthorized input
debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

prompts.prompt: Restate the final input-output contract in one sentence.
Describe the first state where expected and observed behavior diverged.
Explain the repair and the invariant or constraint it restored.
Name one design trade-off and the evidence behind your choice.
What is the safest and most valuable next improvement?

optional_mastery_challenge.title: Optional Mastery Transfer
optional_mastery_challenge.prompt: Transfer the level's eight governing rules to a new version of an accessible browser interface with one changed constraint, one new failure state, and one stricter evidence requirement.
required_outputs: change-impact table across all eight skills
normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery traces
success_criteria: The changed constraint is applied consistently.
No unaffected invariant is silently removed.
The new failure state has visible recovery behavior.
Evidence distinguishes old and new behavior.
